meeting_summary: Follow-up on the 2027-11-02 production incident where Argosy saw intermittent request timeouts and elevated tail latency. Discussed root cause (KV cache churn + autoscaler behavior under bursty traffic), mitigations already applied (temporary autoscaler cap, throttling policy), and next steps for long-term remediation (cache hot-keying fixes, improved autoscaler policy, runbook updates, and a canary window).
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-11-06
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Liu (Redwood AE), Marco Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Reyes (CSM), Diane Harper (Argosy Head of Platform), Ravi Menon (Argosy SRE), Alina Zhou (Argosy Security)

Summary: quick postmortem review, confirm mitigations that were deployed during the incident, align on next steps for permanent fixes and compliance artifacts.

[00:00] Jamie Liu: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to run through the postmortem and make sure the mitigations we pushed are holding and agree next steps. um, i'll start with a quick recap unless diane wants to lead.

[00:15] Diane Harper: no that's fine, jamie. thanks. so quick context - on Nov 2 we started seeing intermittent 500s and timeouts on the inference route. spikes in tail latency led to a cascade of 429s from our app layer. it lasted about 40 minutes total but with several small recurrences overnight.

[00:34] Marco Patel: right, root cause looks like a combination: heavy KV cache eviction due to hot-key churn after the batch-job started at 03:10, plus our autoscaler stepping up new pods which then had cold kv cache misses - so sequential requests hit the model files and we saw high p99. also the autoscaler policy defaulted to aggressive scale-ups which created bursts of cold-cache nodes.

[01:02] Ravi Menon: two quick clarifications - when you say KV cache, you mean the prefix cache in the inference runtime not our redis layer, correct? we had a bit of confusion in the ops runbook.

[01:18] Marco Patel: yes correct - this is internal runtime kv cache (the LRU in the serving process). sometimes the transcriber or doc says KV "cash" or kv cache, sorry for spelling; it's the engine's in-memory KV that holds recent attention states / prefetched prefixes.

[01:35] Alina Zhou: from security/compliance side we flagged that during the incident a set of debugging flags were enabled which created additional logs with user identifiers. we need to ensure retention and redaction are captured for SOC2.

[01:50] Sofia Reyes: noted, alina. we already rotated the debug flags off during the incident but we will provide the audit trail.

[02:05] Jamie Liu: quick timeline - 03:08 first tail-latency increase, 03:12 first 500s, 03:20 we applied temporary autoscaler cap (max 8 nodes), 03:35 throttling policy on the high-throughput route, 03:45 traffic normalized. We also pushed a small config to warm caches on new nodes (preload top-100 keys) - that was a heuristic and reduced p95 but didn't fully eliminate p99 spikes.

[02:45] Diane Harper: can you confirm what the preload heuristics are? we want to understand if preload could ever leak PII or cause other privacy issues.

[03:02] Marco Patel: preload is based on request frequency window - it's purely model prefixes, not user content. we avoid loading recent user prompts. there was a miscommunication earlier in the doc where it sounded like we were preloading user context - not the case.

[03:20] Ravi Menon: okay, that helps. one big ask - can we get a perf plan we can run in our staging that mimics the real burst pattern? the test run we have doesn't create the same hot-key churn.

[03:35] Marco Patel: absolutely - i'll prepare a script that replays prefix distributions and burst arrival rates, plus a variant that forces cold-start churn. i'll include instructions to measure p50/p95/p99 and error rates.

[03:50] Alina Zhou: on the SOC2 front: we need a list of the logs generated, how long they are kept, and confirmation of redaction filters applied. also tell us where debug artifacts are stored and who has access.

[04:05] Sofia Reyes: i'll collect the audit trail and share with alina. jamie will include the incident timeline slides.

[04:20] Diane Harper: wanted to raise a commercial question - given this event, the execs are asking about dedicated vs hosted. is there a short note we can share about whether dedicated capacity would have reduced blast radius?

[04:38] Jamie Liu: yes - short answer: dedicated would reduce noisy neighbor risks and give you more control over autoscaler policies and pre-warming. that said, the core issue was cache churn tied to workload pattern, which can still happen on dedicated unless you tune cache population strategies. dedicated gives more isolation and predictable throughput but it's not a silver bullet. i'll draft a one-pager comparing tradeoffs.

[05:05] Ravi Menon: also curious whether quantization / smaller models might help reduce cold-start time - any thoughts there?

[05:15] Marco Patel: quantization helps for throughput and may reduce memory footprint to keep larger caches resident, but cold-start disk I/O (model load) still dominates unless you use warm-standby or preloaded memory-backed volumes. our runtime has optimizations for quantized kernels but you still need a strategy to keep working set warm.

[05:40] Diane Harper: another ask from legal: we need a formal RCA doc and confirmation we hit no data exfiltration or retention violations. can that be delivered this week?

[05:52] Alina Zhou: yes, we need the security statement up front.

[06:00] Jamie Liu: we'll include a security appendix in the RCA. Marco, can you confirm logs don't include raw prompts beyond the debug window?

[06:12] Marco Patel: confirmed - the logs have hashed request ids and only surface truncated prompt snippets for debugging, we have redaction in place. i'll call out exact fields in the appendix.

[06:28] Ravi Menon: on mitigations - you mentioned a throttling policy. what was the policy threshold and can we tune it?

[06:40] Marco Patel: current throttling was set to 600 req/s for that route, which was our emergency brake while we assessed. longer-term we recommend a smoother token-based backpressure and dynamic batching window so that single spikes don't cause eviction storms. i'll propose concrete numbers in the perf doc.

[07:05] Diane Harper: any regressions observed after we rolled the preload config? e.g., higher memory usage or OOMs?

[07:16] Marco Patel: small uptick in memory footprint but within headroom; no OOMs. metrics show preload reduced average cold-start time by about 18% in the window we measured.

[07:30] Sofia Reyes: i'm tracking customer impact - Argosy logged about 0.6% of requests failing at the peak window, total user-facing errors were minimal but execs want reassurance.

[07:45] Jamie Liu: noted. for exec comms we can include a short blameless timeline, impact numbers, mitigations, and a clear action plan.

[08:00] Diane Harper: would appreciate that. also can you include a proposed SLA credit calculation? it's not final but helps the finance team.

[08:12] Jamie Liu: yes i'll include a draft.

[08:20] Alina Zhou: one more security note - we need attestations around key management for logs and whether debug artifacts ever touched cloud object storage with public links.

[08:32] Marco Patel: they did not. debug artifacts were stored in a restricted logs bucket with enforced IAM, and no public links were created. i'll include IAM snapshot.

[08:45] Diane Harper: great. on the long-term fixes, can you summarize the three-priority list?

[08:52] Marco Patel: sure - P0: fix cache eviction hot-paths (hot-key protection, smarter cache retention). P1: refine autoscaler to avoid mass cold node rollouts and implement graceful pre-warm. P2: improve observability for prefix distributions and add an automatic canary for new scale events.

[09:15] Ravi Menon: timeline expectations for P0/P1?

[09:20] Marco Patel: P0 we can get a code-level mitigation and config out in 2 weeks (target 2027-11-20) and more robust fix in 6-8 weeks. P1 autoscaler tuning and pre-warm could take 3-4 weeks to validate safely. we'll prioritize P0.

[09:40] Diane Harper: ok, that's reasonable. will your perf plan also include a canary gating strategy? we want to avoid surprises on prod.

[09:48] Marco Patel: yes - canary gating will be part of the perf plan and i'll include expected thresholds to roll-back.

[10:02] Sofia Reyes: any blockers on us signing off on the runbook changes? Diane?

[10:10] Diane Harper: i'll need to run it by the on-call SREs and legal for the checklist, but no blockers in principle.

[10:22] Jamie Liu: ok folks we'll recap next steps. i'm going to send the RCA slide deck with timeline, Marco will share the perf/test plan and KV-cache tuning proposals, Sofia will share audit artifacts. then we'll schedule the canary window next week.

[10:45] Ravi Menon: thanks all. one small nit - can you add the exact metric queries for p99 so our dashboards match yours?

[10:55] Marco Patel: yes i'll append the PromQL queries and their labels in the doc.

[11:08] Diane Harper: thanks everyone - that's all from me.

[11:15] Jamie Liu: thanks, we'll follow up over email with the docs.

[11:25] (meeting ends)

References / Links mentioned: RCA slides (link to be shared), perf test script (to be shared), audit trail export (to be shared).
